source.title: From Loops to Oops: Fallback Behaviors of Language Models Under Uncertainty
source.authors: Maor Ivgi; Ori Yoran; Jonathan Berant; Mor Geva

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures factual-answer performance across model sizes, a different measure from the claim’s pretraining-loss scaling laws. It does not measure loss or fit scaling-law predictions.
record.gate_note: The study does not test held-out cross-entropy, power-law fits, extrapolation from smaller runs, compute-optimal allocation, or architectural shape. Its factual-answer counts on TRIVIA FACTS bear on V6, but are not loss measurements. Other reported fallback outcomes (hallucinations, repetitions, decoding and generation-length effects) do not measure a claim version’s named performance relationship.
record.test_reason: The study's focus is fallback behaviours, not scaling laws. Its own Pythia size sweep (70M–12B, same data and order) and checkpoint sweeps report correct-answer counts on factual list recall. That bears on V6: downstream performance improving with scale. It is a new task setting with no loss measurement and no fitted predictive curve, so T3 rather than T1 or T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that hallucinations, degenerate text and repetitions are ordered fallback behaviours under epistemic uncertainty. Stronger models (more parameters, more tokens, instruction tuning) produce more correct facts but shift from repetition toward hallucination. Within a generation, models move from correct facts to hallucinations to repetitions. Sampling trades repetitions for hallucinations. They treat accuracy gains with scale as expected, citing Kaplan, rather than testing scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates factual generation and fallback behaviors rather than measuring held-out loss or fitting scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that fallback outcomes vary with model size, pretraining progress, instruction tuning, decoding method and temperature, prompting, dataset/entity popularity, and generation length.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger, longer-trained and instruction-tuned models shift from repetitions to hallucinations under uncertainty. On FAKE QAMPARI, hallucinations rise from about 15% to over 30% with size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scale changes the type of model errors (repetition to hallucination), not only accuracy.

record.problems: The relevant factual-performance trend is described and shown in a figure, but the flattened figure text does not support reliable assignment of individual values. No loss measurements, fitted performance curve, or predictive validation are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Fallback counts for hallucinations, repetitions, topic changes and formatting errors, plus decoding, prompt, instruction-tuning and generation-length results, were omitted because they do not measure the performance relationship named by V6 or any other listed version.

untested.parts: Prediction from pretraining loss; a fitted functional form; extrapolation to larger models; conventional benchmarks.
Not measured: no held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fits in parameters, tokens or compute.
Not measured: no power laws fitted on small runs used to predict larger runs.
Not measured: no compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens.
Not measured: no depth, width or other architecture-shape comparisons.
Not measured: no other modalities or regimes (repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer).
Not measured: no comparison of fitting choices or setups.

missing.what: Correct-answer counts across pretraining checkpoints (tokens seen), e.g. Pythia-6.9B rising from about 1.7 at 2B tokens to 4.1 at 300B. Similar results for Pythia-12B and OLMo-1B/7B.
Correct counts vs size for OLMo, Llama 2 and Llama 3 on TRIVIA FACTS, and for all families on QAMPARI.
Correct atomic facts vs Pythia size (2.8B/6.9B/12B) on BIO GENERATION by entity popularity.
Size trend under temperature 0.5 sampling and the colon-prompt variant.

record.verdict_notes: Accuracy-with-scale is incidental to the paper's aim, and the evidence is monotone improvement, not 'predictable' improvement. Per-model values come from flattened figure labels whose bar mapping is ambiguous. Researchers should check Figs 2, 9 and 17 or the released results at github.com/Mivg/fallbacks. The plateau verdict rests on these approximate numbers.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and range.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocations under fixed compute, and their scaling with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss in other modalities or regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The study tests factual-answer counts on TRIVIA FACTS across Pythia model sizes, but not performance across conventional downstream benchmarks, prediction from pretraining loss, or a fitted predictive relationship.
Dependence of fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and bending of loss curves.

relationships.reason: Authors state larger models recall more correct answers. Flattened labels show correct counts rising from about 2–3 to about 4.1 (r1–r7).
